Japan.permitName: Entertainer (Kogyo) status of residence, via Certificate of Eligibility
Japan.summary: Paid shows are not allowed on visa-free or Temporary Visitor entry. The Japanese promoter or venue gets a Certificate of Eligibility for 'Entertainer' status, then the artist gets the visa or enters on it.
Japan.cost: Certificate of Eligibility is free; consular visa fee varies by nationality
steps: Promoter files the Certificate of Eligibility at its regional immigration bureau with the contract and the artist's credentials
Promoter sends the certificate to the artist
Artist applies for the visa at a Japanese embassy if their nationality needs one, or shows the certificate on arrival
Japanese payer withholds tax from the fee
Japan.tax: Japanese payer withholds 20.42% of the fee (20% plus reconstruction surtax); a tax treaty may reduce it if filed in advance

South Korea.permitName: E-6 Arts and Entertainment visa (E-6-1; E-6-2 for some hotel/bar-type venues)
South Korea.summary: Paid shows are not allowed on visa-free or K-ETA entry. The Korean organiser gets a Korea Media Rating Board recommendation where the venue requires one, then sponsors an E-6 visa.
steps: Organiser applies to the Korea Media Rating Board for a performance recommendation (around 1-2 weeks)
Organiser applies for a Visa Issuance Confirmation at Korean immigration
Artist collects the E-6 visa at a Korean consulate or e-visa
Korean payer withholds tax from the fee

China.permitName: Commercial performance approval plus Z (work) visa
China.summary: Visa-free entry does not cover paid shows. A licensed Chinese performance agency must get the culture authority's approval for foreign commercial performances, then the artist applies for a Z visa.
steps: Local licensed performance agency applies to the culture and tourism authority for approval of the show
Agency issues the visa invitation/notification letter with the approval
Artist applies for a Z visa at a Chinese embassy or visa centre
The approved line-up, dates and venues must be followed

Hong Kong.permitName: Employment visa / entry permit for entertainers
Hong Kong.summary: Visitors may not perform for pay, whatever the length of stay. The local promoter sponsors an employment visa for entertainers. A 14-day facilitation scheme exists only for guests of approved host organisations.
Hong Kong.exemptNote: The Short-term Activities (STV) scheme lets guests of authorised host organisations in sectors like Arts and Cultural work up to 14 days without a visa. It is unlikely to cover ordinary club bookings.
steps: Hong Kong promoter sponsors the employment visa / entry permit application with ImmD
Artist enters only after the visa is approved
Hong Kong payer withholds tax and files the return for the artist
Hong Kong.tax: Payer withholds 10% of the gross fee for individuals (about 11% if paid to a foreign company), as a prepayment of profits tax

Taiwan.permitName: Work permit for foreign professionals in arts and performing arts (Ministry of Labor)
Taiwan.summary: Paid gigs need a Ministry of Labor arts and performance work permit, even on visa-free entry. The Taiwanese organiser applies before the show.
Taiwan.exemptNote: Some short stays of 30 days or less are treated as work-permitted, for example non-profit performances invited by the central government. Do not assume a paid club show qualifies.
steps: Organiser applies online to the Workforce Development Agency for an arts/performance work permit
Artist enters visa-free or with a visitor visa once the permit is issued
Taiwanese payer withholds tax from the fee

Singapore.permitName: Work Pass Exempt Activity notification, or a work pass for nightlife venues
Singapore.summary: Shows at public performance venues or government-supported events can run on a visit pass if MOM is notified first. Bars, clubs, lounges and hotels with a Category 1 entertainment licence are excluded, and the Performing Artiste Work Permit closed to new applications on 1 June 2026, so club bookings need a regular work pass or a service-provider arrangement.
Singapore.exemptNote: Exempt-activity route: up to 90 days a year in total. Not valid for performances at bars, discotheques, lounges, nightclubs, pubs, hotels, private clubs or restaurants with a Category 1 licence.
steps: Check whether the venue is a public performance venue or a Category 1 licensed nightlife venue
Festival or concert venue: enter on a Short-Term Visit Pass, then notify MOM online before the show
Nightclub or bar: ask MOM or the venue which work pass now applies before booking flights
Singapore payer withholds 15% tax and files with IRAS
Singapore.tax: 15% withholding on non-resident public entertainers' fees (the 10% concession ended 31 March 2022)

Thailand.permitName: Work permit (Ministry of Labour) with Non-Immigrant B visa
Thailand.summary: Performing, even unpaid, counts as work, so visa-exempt entry is not enough. A Thai club, festival or agency sponsors a work permit, and the artist usually enters on a Non-Immigrant B visa.
steps: Thai organiser prepares the sponsor documents and work permit application
Artist gets a Non-Immigrant B visa at a Thai embassy before travel
Work permit is finalised once the artist is in Thailand, before the show
Thai payer withholds tax from the fee

Indonesia.permitName: Performer visit visa (C7 / C7A music performance e-visa)
Indonesia.summary: Visa-on-arrival and visa-free entry do not cover paid shows. The Indonesian organiser sponsors a performer e-visa (usually single-entry, about 30 days) before the artist flies.
steps: Organiser applies as sponsor on evisa.imigrasi.go.id with the event details and the artist's profile
Artist receives the e-visa before travelling
Payment usually runs through a contract between the local sponsor and the artist's company
Indonesian payer withholds tax from the fee

Philippines.permitName: Special Work Permit (SWP), Bureau of Immigration
Philippines.summary: Foreign artists performing in front of an audience for a fee need a Special Work Permit. The local promoter files for it on the artist's behalf before the event.
steps: Promoter files the SWP petition with the Bureau of Immigration (the rules say at least 3 working days before the show; allow more)
Artist enters visa-free or on a visa, depending on nationality
Promoter withholds tax and remits it to the BIR

Vietnam.permitName: Performance licence/approval (performing arts authority) plus a work-purpose visa
Vietnam.summary: Shows with foreign performers need approval from the culture authorities, and the artist needs a visa that allows the activity (tourist e-visa is not enough). Work permit exemptions for short stays exist under Decree 393/2026, but how they apply to DJs is unclear.
steps: Vietnamese organiser gets performance approval for the show and the foreign line-up
Organiser handles any work permit exemption confirmation needed
Organiser sponsors the artist's visa with the immigration department
Local payer withholds personal income tax

Malaysia.permitName: PUSPAL approval plus Professional Visit Pass
Malaysia.summary: Every foreign artiste performance needs approval from PUSPAL (One-Stop Centre for Foreign Film Production and Foreign Artiste Performances), followed by a Professional Visit Pass. The Malaysian organiser applies.
steps: Organiser applies online via ePUSPAL with the event, venue and artist details
After PUSPAL approval, organiser applies to Immigration for the Professional Visit Pass
Local police and council permits for the event may also be needed
Malaysian payer withholds tax from the fee
Malaysia.tax: 15% withholding on fees paid to non-resident public entertainers

India.summary: Tourist or business e-visas do not allow paid performances. Foreign artists usually need an Employment visa supported by the Indian organiser's contract, and some states need local event permissions.
India.exemptNote: Citizens of Nepal and Bhutan do not need a visa for India. Check whether paid work still needs other clearances.
steps: Indian organiser issues the contract and supporting letter
Artist applies for an Employment visa at an Indian mission or visa centre
Organiser arranges local event permissions
Indian payer withholds tax from the fee
India.tax: Non-resident entertainers are taxed at 20% of gross receipts plus surcharge and cess (s.115BBA), withheld by the payer (s.194E)

Australia.permitName: Temporary Activity visa (subclass 408), Entertainment activities stream
Australia.summary: ETA and eVisitor do not allow paid shows. The Australian promoter is usually an approved Temporary Activities Sponsor and nominates the artist, who then applies for a 408 visa.
Australia.cost: Visa charge set by Home Affairs (check the Visa Pricing Estimator); sponsor approval is separate
Australia.exemptNote: New Zealand citizens can work in Australia on the Special Category visa (subclass 444) granted on arrival.
steps: Promoter gets Temporary Activities Sponsor approval if it doesn't already have it
Promoter lodges the sponsorship and nominates the artist
Artist lodges the 408 visa application online and waits for the grant before travelling
Australian payer withholds tax under the ATO's foreign resident rules
Australia.tax: Payer must withhold from fees to foreign-resident entertainers (company rate for companies, foreign-resident individual rate for individuals, top rate without an ABN); a variation can be requested from the ATO

New Zealand.permitName: Short-term Entertainment Act Visitor Visa (or NZeTA with approved-promoter letter)
New Zealand.summary: Short live shows are allowed when the promoter is on Immigration New Zealand's approved list. Visa-waiver nationals can use an NZeTA with the promoter's letter; others need the Short-term Entertainment Act Visitor Visa.
New Zealand.exemptNote: Australian citizens may live and work in New Zealand without a work visa. If the promoter is not approved, a work visa (for example the Entertainers Work Visa) is needed.
steps: Check that the promoter holds Immigration New Zealand approved-promoter status
Promoter issues the invitation/support letter
Visa-waiver nationals request an NZeTA at least 72 hours before travel; others apply for the visitor visa at least 4 weeks ahead
Anyone with criminal convictions must apply for a visa
New Zealand.tax: NZ payers generally deduct non-resident withholding (schedular) tax from entertainer fees; confirm the current rate with Inland Revenue

United Kingdom.permitName: Standard Visitor - Permitted Paid Engagement (PPE); Permit-Free Festival; Creative Worker visa / concession
United Kingdom.summary: Non-visa nationals can play paid UK shows as a visitor under Permitted Paid Engagement if invited by a UK promoter and the gig is within 30 days of arrival; they need an ETA, not a visa. Visa nationals must get a Standard Visitor visa before travel; longer or multi-show tours use the Creative Worker route with a Certificate of Sponsorship.
United Kingdom.exemptNote: Not a visa, but still conditional: written invitation from a UK client, evidence you are an established professional, paid by a UK source, engagement done within 30 days of entry. ETA needed by all of these except Irish citizens. Tell Border Force you are on a PPE; do not rely on eGates. Visa nationals relevant to club music include China, India, South Africa, Colombia, Turkey, Georgia, Thailand, Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Nigeria, Egypt, Russia, Ukraine.
steps: Get a signed invitation letter from the UK promoter/venue naming dates and fee
Non-visa nationals: apply for a UK ETA online; visa nationals: apply for a Standard Visitor visa (state PPE) well before travel
Carry the invitation plus proof of your profession (press, past gig listings) and see a Border Force officer on arrival
For tours longer than 30 days or with a sponsor, use a Creative Worker Certificate of Sponsorship
United Kingdom.tax: UK payer must withhold basic-rate tax (20%) via HMRC's Foreign Entertainers Unit once total UK payments to the artist exceed the personal allowance; reduced rate possible via form FEU8 (30 days ahead).

Germany.permitName: Exemption under §22 + §30 Employment Ordinance (BeschV): one-day performances up to 15 days a year; festivals/guest performances up to 90 days in 12 months
Germany.summary: Short club and festival shows by artists who live abroad do not count as employment, so no work permit is needed. Visa-free nationals just enter; visa-required nationals still need a Schengen short-stay visa.
Germany.exemptNote: Artist must keep their usual residence abroad. Single-day shows: max 15 performance days per calendar year; festivals and guest performances: max 90 days in 12 months. Schengen 90/180-day rule applies. ETIAS pre-travel authorisation expected for visa-free travellers from late 2026.
steps: Check the gigs fit the 15-days-a-year (single shows) or 90-days (festival/tour) limit
Visa-required nationals: apply for a Schengen C visa at the German mission with contract and invitation
Carry the performance contract at the border
Agree with the promoter how the §50a withholding tax is handled
Germany.tax: Promoter withholds 15% plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge (15.825%) on fees to non-resident artists under §50a EStG; no withholding for fees up to EUR 250 per performance. Treaty relief needs a BZSt exemption certificate.

France.permitName: Work-authorisation exemption for stays of 3 months or less in cultural and artistic events (Code du travail L5221-2-1 / D5221-2-1)
France.summary: Non-EU artists playing shows in France for 3 months or less need no work authorisation. Visa-required nationals still need a Schengen short-stay visa, and the promoter must contract and pay the artist properly (usually as a salaried performer).
France.exemptNote: Covers performers and production crew on contracts of 3 months or less. Schengen 90/180-day rule applies. In France performers are presumed employees, so the promoter normally pays via a work contract (e.g. GUSO) unless a foreign company invoices.
steps: Get the contract from the French promoter (usually an employment contract for the performance)
Visa-required nationals: apply for a Schengen C visa at the French consulate/France-Visas
Carry the contract and invitation at the border
France.tax: 15% withholding on artistic fees paid to non-residents (CGI art. 182 A bis), after a 10% deduction for expenses; tax treaties can change this.

Netherlands.permitName: Work-permit (TWV/GVVA) exemption for musicians and artists: max 6 consecutive weeks within 13 weeks
Netherlands.summary: Foreign musicians and artists can perform in the Netherlands without a work permit for up to 6 consecutive weeks in a 13-week period. Visa-required nationals still need a Schengen short-stay visa.
Netherlands.exemptNote: Limit is 6 consecutive weeks in any 13 weeks; leaving and re-entering within that window may trigger a permit requirement. Non-EU crew may not be covered. Schengen 90/180-day rule applies.
steps: Confirm the stay fits the 6-weeks-in-13 limit
Visa-required nationals: apply for a Schengen C visa at the Dutch mission
Send the promoter your tax residence certificate if you want treaty relief

Spain.permitName: Work authorisation (Ley Orgánica 4/2000 and Reglamento RD 1155/2024); former exemption for one-off artist performances
Spain.summary: Spain used to exempt artists playing one-off shows (up to 5 consecutive days or 20 days in 6 months) from a work permit; practitioner guides say the new 2025 regulation no longer clearly lists this exemption. Check with the promoter or a Spanish immigration lawyer before booking.
Spain.exemptNote: Status of the short-performance exemption under RD 1155/2024 (in force 20 May 2025) is unclear. Visa-free nationals can enter without a Schengen visa but other obligations (NIE, social security registration by promoter, tax) may still apply.
steps: Ask the Spanish promoter to confirm in writing whether a work authorisation is needed for your dates
Visa-required nationals: apply for a Schengen C visa or the visa the promoter's authorisation specifies
Make sure the promoter handles social security registration and IRNR tax withholding

Italy.permitName: Nulla osta / work visa for performing artists (Testo Unico Immigrazione art. 27; DPR 394/99 art. 40 c.15 for self-employed stays under 90 days)
Italy.summary: Non-EU artists generally need a work visa for paid performances in Italy, normally based on a nulla osta requested by the Italian organiser or, for short self-employed jobs, on the contract. Rules are complex; get the promoter to handle it early.
Italy.exemptNote: No clear official short-stay exemption for artists was found; visa-free entry alone does not authorise paid work.
steps: Italian organiser requests the nulla osta (or prepares the contract for a self-employed work visa)
Artist applies for the work visa at the Italian consulate with the nulla osta or contract
Enter within the visa's validity and perform only for the named organiser
Italy.tax: 30% final withholding on fees paid to non-resident performers (DPR 600/73 art. 25); treaties may change this. Travel/hotel paid as buy-outs are often taxed too.

Portugal.permitName: Temporary stay visa for professional performing activity (visto de estada temporária para espetáculos); Schengen short-stay visa for up to 90 days
Portugal.summary: Portugal has a dedicated visa for performers; official guidance points stays of up to 90 days to the Schengen short-stay route. Whether visa-free nationals can play a 1-3 night paid show without any authorisation is not clearly stated, so check with AIMA or the consulate.
Portugal.exemptNote: No explicit short-stay artist exemption found in official sources.

Visa-required nationals: apply at the Portuguese consulate at least 30 days before travel
Carry the performance contract

Belgium.summary: Artists with an international reputation are exempt from a work permit for short stays: up to 21 days per quarter in Flanders, and up to 90 days per quarter in Brussels and Wallonia. Visa-required nationals still need a Schengen visa and the employer may need a Limosa declaration.
Belgium.exemptNote: Only if the artist counts as internationally renowned; keep proof (contract, press, CV). Flanders 21 days per quarter; Brussels/Wallonia 90 days per quarter (secondary source). A Limosa declaration may be required.
steps: Check which region the venue is in and that the stay fits its day limit
Prepare proof of international reputation
Promoter/employer files a Limosa declaration if required
Visa-required nationals: apply for a Schengen C visa

Poland.permitName: Work-permit exemption for artistic performances up to 30 days per calendar year
Poland.summary: Foreign artists performing musical or stage work in Poland need no work permit for up to 30 days in a calendar year, provided they are legally in Poland. Visa-required nationals still need a Schengen short-stay visa.
Poland.exemptNote: Max 30 days per calendar year (regulation in force from 1 Dec 2025); legal stay required (visa-free entry, visa or residence permit).

Visa-required nationals: apply for a Schengen C visa at the Polish consulate
Carry the contract at the border

Czech Republic.summary: Performing artists need no work permit if each stay of work is no more than 7 consecutive days and 30 days total per calendar year. Visa-required nationals still need a Schengen short-stay visa.
Czech Republic.exemptNote: Limits: 7 consecutive days and 30 days per calendar year. Longer tours need an employment permit.
steps: Check the dates fit 7 consecutive days / 30 days a year

Carry the contract at the border

Turkey.permitName: Work permit exemption for scientific, cultural and artistic activities (Implementing Regulation art. 48/a), max 1 month

Turkey.exemptNote: The 1-month exemption is not automatic: it is granted via the Ministry of Labour system. Some nationalities are visa-exempt for entry, but still need the exemption to work.

UAE.permitName: Performer / entertainment permit (Dubai: DET e-permit; Abu Dhabi: DCT) plus entry visa
UAE.summary: Every DJ or live act at a public or ticketed event needs an individual performer permit, applied for by a locally licensed organiser through the emirate's permit system. The artist also needs a valid entry visa unless visa-free.
UAE.exemptNote: Rules and authorities differ by emirate; mostly documented by agencies, not in official public guidance.

Promoter applies for the performer permit via the DET (Dubai) or DCT (Abu Dhabi) system

United States.permitName: O-1B, P-1B or P-3 visa (Form I-129 petition)
United States.summary: Paid shows are not allowed on ESTA or a B-1/B-2 visitor visa. A US petitioner (promoter, venue or agent) must get an approved I-129 petition from USCIS, then the artist gets the visa at a US consulate.
United States.exemptNote: No nationality is exempt from the petition. Canadian citizens still need an approved petition but no visa stamp.

Allow 2-6 months; premium processing gives a decision in about 15 business days

Plan US tax withholding or a Central Withholding Agreement with the IRS

Canada.permitName: Work-permit exemption for performing artists (IRPR R186(g))
Canada.summary: Foreign DJs and performers can play short, time-limited paid gigs in Canada without a work permit, as long as they are not employed by the venue. They still need a normal eTA or visitor visa to enter.
Canada.cost: No work permit fee; eTA CAD 7 or visitor visa fee if your nationality needs one
Canada.exemptNote: The exemption covers all nationalities. It does not apply to an employment relationship (e.g. a residency several nights a week for weeks) or to film/TV/radio productions.
steps: Get an eTA or visitor visa, depending on nationality
Carry the performance contract and itinerary for the border officer
Keep the booking short and freelance (no employment contract with the venue)
Expect 15% withholding on the fee unless a waiver is approved
Canada.tax: 15% non-resident withholding on fees for services in Canada (Income Tax Regulation 105); a waiver can be requested from CRA. Provincial withholding may also apply.

Mexico.permitName: Visitor visa with permission to carry out paid activities (Visitante con permiso para realizar actividades remuneradas)
Mexico.summary: Tourist entry does not allow paid work. The Mexican promoter must get an INM authorisation first, then the artist collects the paid-activity visitor visa at a Mexican consulate.
Mexico.cost: Consular visa fee plus INM migration fee; amounts vary, check the consulate
Mexico.exemptNote: Consulates say all foreign nationals hired to perform need the INM permit, including those who are visa-exempt as tourists.

INM decision usually takes about 30 days
Artist books a consulate appointment within 30 days of the INM letter and gets the visa (2-10 working days)
Promoter withholds Mexican tax on the fee

Brazil.permitName: Visit visa (Visto de visita, VIVIS) or visa-exempt entry; temporary visa for longer fixed-term contracts
Brazil.summary: Brazil's Migration Law lets visitors receive a performance fee (cachê) for short artistic activities, so visa-exempt nationals can usually play on normal entry. Nationals who need a visa (incl. US, Canada, Australia since April 2025) must get a visit visa or e-visa first.
Brazil.exemptNote: These nationals do not need a visa for short visits, and visitors may be paid a cachê under Law 13.445 Art. 13. Most other EU countries are also visa-exempt; check Itamaraty's list. Longer fixed-term contracts need a temporary visa.
steps: Check Itamaraty's visa table for the artist's nationality
If a visa is needed, apply for the visit visa or e-visa with the promoter's invitation and contract
Carry the contract showing a short, time-limited engagement
Promoter withholds Brazilian income tax on the fee

Argentina.summary: Paid artistic work needs a transitory permit from the National Migration Directorate (DNM). It is requested through a local organiser registered in RENURE and is valid for up to one month.
Argentina.cost: DNM migration fee per the official fee table; amount not confirmed
Argentina.exemptNote: Not confirmed whether Mercosur nationals can skip this for a one-off show; check with DNM.

Organiser files the electronic entry request with a notarised note and the contract
Artist shows the DNM authorisation email to the officer on arrival

Colombia.permitName: Permit for Other Activities (POA) - concerts, events or artistic activities; Visitor visa (Visa V) for visa-required nationals
Colombia.summary: Visa-exempt artists still need a POA from Migración Colombia for concerts and artistic events, requested online at least 5 business days before arrival. Artists from visa-required countries need a Visitor (V) visa from the Foreign Ministry.
Colombia.exemptNote: No nationality is exempt from the POA. A plain tourist entry (PIP) does not allow being paid in Colombia.
steps: Check whether the artist's nationality needs a visa for Colombia
Visa-exempt: file the POA form on Migración Colombia ('Conciertos, eventos o actividades artísticas') 5+ business days ahead
Visa-required: apply for the Visa V at Cancillería with the organiser's invitation
Ask the promoter about non-resident withholding on the fee

Chile.permitName: Work authorisation for Permanencia Transitoria holders (Autorización para trabajar con Permanencia Transitoria)
Chile.summary: Tourists cannot be paid without permission. Performers at public shows can get a short work authorisation from SERMIG for the exact show dates, filed online before or after arrival.
Chile.cost: SERMIG fee per the official tariff (amount varies by nationality)
steps: Get a notarised letter or contract from the Chilean promoter with duties, venue and exact dates
File on SERMIG's online portal (artist, representative or employer), no later than the business day before the show
Pay the fee and carry the approval at the gig
Promoter withholds Chilean tax on the fee

sources.title: SERMIG: Autorización de trabajo para titulares de Permanencia Transitoria
ChileAtiende: Autorización para trabajar con Permanencia Transitoria

South Africa.permitName: Visitor's visa with Section 11(2) short-term work authorisation
South Africa.summary: Any paid work, including short gigs, needs a Section 11(2) work authorisation, even for visa-exempt nationals. Apply at a South African embassy before travelling, with a letter from the local host.
South Africa.cost: Small mission fee where applicable (e.g. AUD 37 in Canberra)
South Africa.exemptNote: Visa-exempt nationals still need the Section 11(2) authorisation for paid work; the authorisation is capped at 90 days per stay.
steps: Get a letter from the South African promoter to the Director-General of Home Affairs describing the work and dates
Apply in person at the South African mission for your country with Form DHA-84 and documents
Allow about 10 working days processing
Promoter withholds 15% entertainer tax and pays it to SARS
